html:
This territory marks the Nahua peoples of central and eastern Mexico, in today's states of Morelos, Puebla, Tlaxcala, Veracruz, Hidalgo and San Luis Potosí. The Nahua speak Nahuatl, the language of the Aztecs, still the most spoken Indigenous language in Mexico, with about 1.6 million speakers.

In 1492 most of this land paid tribute to the Aztec Triple Alliance. Nahua city-states in Morelos and Puebla sent cotton, cloth and food to Tenochtitlan. The one large exception was Tlaxcala, a Nahua republic in the hills east of the valley of Mexico that the Aztecs fought for decades but never conquered.

When Hernán Cortés landed in 1519, the Tlaxcalans fought him and then joined him, and thousands of them marched in the siege that brought the fall of Tenochtitlan in 1521. Under Spanish rule Nahua towns kept their councils and wrote records in Nahuatl in the Latin alphabet. Neighbours include the Totonac and Huastec. See also Nahua (Mexico).
